title: Riverglass Expedition of 1928
license: Apache-2.0 (original fictional teaching text, Research Explorer)

parts.heading: Overview
parts.text: The Riverglass Expedition of 1928 is a fictional field campaign in which four members of Riverglass Observatory carried a portable transit instrument across the Ostmere salt flats to compare star timings taken far from the river fog. It is part of the original Research Explorer teaching collection and describes no real expedition.

parts.heading: Background
parts.text: By the 1920s ferry pilots had begun to question whether the observatory's tide-star times were affected by mist over the Tamsel. The society's director, Ines Varga, proposed repeating a series of timings on the dry Ostmere plateau, where the sky was reliably clear.

parts.heading: Route
parts.text: The party left Riverglass on 2 August 1928 with two carts, the portable transit and a ship's chronometer borrowed from the ferry company.

parts.heading: Ostmere crossing
parts.text: The crossing took nine days. The surveyors marked their route with cairns so that the chronometer could be carried back along a measured line, allowing them to estimate how much it drifted on the journey.

parts.heading: Camp Lantern
parts.text: The observing camp, named Camp Lantern after the shaded lamps used for reading the wires, stood forty kilometres east of the observatory. Tobiah Lusk later described the cold nights there in his memoir.

parts.heading: Observations
parts.text: Over sixteen clear nights the party timed eleven tide-stars. The camp results agreed with the observatory's catalogue to within a fraction of a second for ten of them, supporting the view that the river fog had little effect on the published times.

parts.heading: Disputed reading
parts.text: The expedition compared two readings of the star Ferryman's Lamp taken at the camp and at the observatory on the same night. They differed by 1.8 seconds, far more than the other ten stars. Mira Carrow, the expedition's computer, argued in a letter that the chronometer had been jolted on the crossing; Lusk maintained that the observatory clock was at fault. The question was never settled.

parts.heading: Aftermath
parts.text: The expedition's results were printed as an appendix to the fourth edition of the Tide-Star Catalogue. The disputed reading was published with both explanations side by side, following the founding rule that observations are printed with their observers' names.
